name: Back pain that prefers bending
explanation: Your back is sensitive to sustained arching or standing. Comfortable bending and gradually rebuilding strength may help.
course: Often improves over several weeks with a manageable, consistent routine. Persistent symptoms can still improve; progress is not always linear.
helps: Start with a dose you can recover from. Use the next-morning response to guide load, then build strength gradually.
cue: Comfortable bending is your friend here — we use it to unload the joint surfaces.

name: Back pain that prefers straightening
explanation: Sitting and bending seem to irritate your back. Short, comfortable movement in the opposite direction may help.
course: Often improves over several weeks with a manageable, consistent routine. Persistent symptoms can still improve; progress is not always linear.
helps: Start with a dose you can recover from. Use the next-morning response to guide load, then build strength gradually.
cue: Straightening eases you, so we keep the low back long and avoid sustained slumping.

name: Back pain with sensitive leg nerves
explanation: A sensitive nerve can cause pain or tingling that travels into a leg. Start with movements that keep symptoms closer to your back, not farther down your leg.
course: Often improves over several weeks with a manageable, consistent routine. Persistent symptoms can still improve; progress is not always linear.
helps: Start with a dose you can recover from. Use the next-morning response to guide load, then build strength gradually.
nameAr: ألم أسفل الظهر مع تحسس العصب
cue: Nerves do not like being stretched hard. We move within a range that leaves the leg calm.

name: Pain around the back of your pelvis
explanation: Pain close to the pelvic joints can be sensitive to uneven loading. Comfortable, even-sided movement and gradual hip strength may help.
course: Often improves over several weeks with a manageable, consistent routine. Persistent symptoms can still improve; progress is not always linear.
helps: Start with a dose you can recover from. Use the next-morning response to guide load, then build strength gradually.
cue: Symmetry and steady loading suit this joint: avoid long strides and heavy twisting at first.

name: A sensitive, stiff neck
explanation: Neck movement can become uncomfortable after an awkward load or position. Gentle movement and gradual strength usually help.
course: Often improves over several weeks with a manageable, consistent routine. Persistent symptoms can still improve; progress is not always linear.
helps: Start with a dose you can recover from. Use the next-morning response to guide load, then build strength gradually.
cue: Small, frequent, comfortable movement. Cracking or end-range stretching is not the goal.

name: Neck discomfort with sustained positions
explanation: Long periods in one position can tire the neck and shoulders. Regular movement breaks matter more than finding a perfect posture.
course: Often improves over several weeks with a manageable, consistent routine. Persistent symptoms can still improve; progress is not always linear.
helps: Start with a dose you can recover from. Use the next-morning response to guide load, then build strength gradually.
cue: Holding one position is the trigger, not the position itself — we change shape often.

name: Headache linked to neck movement
explanation: Some headaches change with neck position or movement. Easy neck mobility can help, but new or unusual headaches need an assessment.
course: Often improves over several weeks with a manageable, consistent routine. Persistent symptoms can still improve; progress is not always linear.
helps: Start with a dose you can recover from. Use the next-morning response to guide load, then build strength gradually.
cue: These headaches usually start in the upper neck, so we move the neck, not the head only.

name: Neck pain with sensitive arm nerves
explanation: Pain or tingling travelling into the arm can reflect nerve sensitivity. Avoid movements that spread symptoms farther down the arm.
course: Often improves over several weeks with a manageable, consistent routine. Persistent symptoms can still improve; progress is not always linear.
helps: Start with a dose you can recover from. Use the next-morning response to guide load, then build strength gradually.
nameAr: ألم رقبة مع تحسس أعصب اليد
cue: If tingling travels further down the arm, we shorten the range immediately.

name: A shoulder sensitive to load
explanation: The muscles and tendons supporting your shoulder may be sensitive to reaching and lifting. A manageable amount of loading can build their tolerance.
course: Often improves over several weeks with a manageable, consistent routine. Persistent symptoms can still improve; progress is not always linear.
helps: Start with a dose you can recover from. Use the next-morning response to guide load, then build strength gradually.
cue: Load the cuff before you load the range. Pain-free early, full range later.

name: Pain when raising your arm
explanation: Reaching overhead can irritate a sensitive shoulder. Comfortable movement and gradual shoulder strength can improve confidence and capacity.
course: Often improves over several weeks with a manageable, consistent routine. Persistent symptoms can still improve; progress is not always linear.
helps: Start with a dose you can recover from. Use the next-morning response to guide load, then build strength gradually.
cue: The painful arc is usually in the middle. We train below it and above it, not inside it.

name: A shoulder becoming stiff in several directions
explanation: A slowly stiffening shoulder, including difficulty turning the arm outwards, can need a gentler approach. Avoid forcing stretches or heavy strengthening while it is very painful.
course: Often changes over many months. Comfort and useful movement matter more than forcing range.
helps: Start with a dose you can recover from. Use the next-morning response to guide load, then build strength gradually.
cue: Stiffness in several directions means we protect the joint: no strengthening until it settles.

name: Pain at the top of your shoulder
explanation: The small joint at the top of your shoulder can be sensitive to crossing your arm or lying on that side. Adjust the load while keeping comfortable movement.
course: Often improves over several weeks with a manageable, consistent routine. Persistent symptoms can still improve; progress is not always linear.
helps: Start with a dose you can recover from. Use the next-morning response to guide load, then build strength gradually.
cue: Reaching across the body is the provocative direction, so we keep the arm in front of you.

name: Pain around the kneecap
explanation: Stairs, squats or long sitting can be uncomfortable when the kneecap area is sensitive. Gradual hip and knee loading can build tolerance.
course: Often improves over several weeks with a manageable, consistent routine. Persistent symptoms can still improve; progress is not always linear.
helps: Start with a dose you can recover from. Use the next-morning response to guide load, then build strength gradually.
cue: We build the quadriceps in the range that does not press the kneecap in hard.

name: A kneecap tendon sensitive to load
explanation: Jumping and faster loading can irritate the tendon below the kneecap. Start with manageable loading, then rebuild spring and speed.
course: Often improves over several weeks with a manageable, consistent routine. Persistent symptoms can still improve; progress is not always linear.
helps: Start with a dose you can recover from. Use the next-morning response to guide load, then build strength gradually.
cue: Tendons like slow, heavy, predictable load. Total rest usually makes the next day worse.

name: A knee sensitive to twisting
explanation: A sensitive knee can dislike deep bending and rotation. Comfortable movement and strength help; true locking needs an assessment.
course: Often improves over several weeks with a manageable, consistent routine. Persistent symptoms can still improve; progress is not always linear.
helps: Start with a dose you can recover from. Use the next-morning response to guide load, then build strength gradually.
cue: Deep squatting and twisting together is the aggravating pattern, so we separate them.

name: A stiff knee that eases with movement
explanation: A knee that stiffens after rest often benefits from regular gentle movement and progressive strength. Symptoms do not tell us how much structural change is present.
course: Often improves over several weeks with a manageable, consistent routine. Persistent symptoms can still improve; progress is not always linear.
helps: Start with a dose you can recover from. Use the next-morning response to guide load, then build strength gradually.
cue: Stiffness eases with movement, so the first minutes are a warm-up, not a waste.

name: Pain on the outside of your hip
explanation: The outer hip tendons may be sensitive to compression and load. Avoid hanging on one hip and build strength without squeezing the painful side.
course: Often improves over several weeks with a manageable, consistent routine. Persistent symptoms can still improve; progress is not always linear.
helps: Start with a dose you can recover from. Use the next-morning response to guide load, then build strength gradually.
cue: Compression matters more than weakness: we reduce time on that side before adding load.

name: A hip that feels stiff after rest
explanation: Hip stiffness often responds to regular comfortable movement and strength. Keep useful movement in your day and build gradually.
course: Often improves over several weeks with a manageable, consistent routine. Persistent symptoms can still improve; progress is not always linear.
helps: Start with a dose you can recover from. Use the next-morning response to guide load, then build strength gradually.
cue: Stiffness after sitting eases with movement; end-range grinding is not a goal.

name: A groin sensitive after activity
explanation: The muscles around your groin can become sensitive after a change in activity or a strain. Begin with easy contractions before returning to faster movements.
course: Often improves over several weeks with a manageable, consistent routine. Persistent symptoms can still improve; progress is not always linear.
helps: Start with a dose you can recover from. Use the next-morning response to guide load, then build strength gradually.
cue: Adduction is loaded early but slowly — this area is stubborn when rushed.

name: An ankle recovering from a twist
explanation: After a twist, comfortable motion and gradually returning weight through the ankle can help. Major swelling or inability to bear weight needs assessment.
course: Often improves over several weeks with a manageable, consistent routine. Persistent symptoms can still improve; progress is not always linear.
helps: Start with a dose you can recover from. Use the next-morning response to guide load, then build strength gradually.
cue: Balance work is not a bonus here: it is how the ankle learns to trust the ground again.

name: An Achilles tendon sensitive to load
explanation: The tendon behind the ankle may be sensitive to sudden increases in walking or running. Consistent slow calf loading builds tolerance.
course: Often improves over several weeks with a manageable, consistent routine. Persistent symptoms can still improve; progress is not always linear.
helps: Start with a dose you can recover from. Use the next-morning response to guide load, then build strength gradually.
cue: Heel raises are the treatment, not the risk — but slow, and never first thing in the morning.

name: Heel pain on your first steps
explanation: The tissues under the heel may be sensitive after rest and long periods of standing. Comfortable foot and calf loading can help.
course: Often improves over several weeks with a manageable, consistent routine. Persistent symptoms can still improve; progress is not always linear.
helps: Start with a dose you can recover from. Use the next-morning response to guide load, then build strength gradually.
cue: First-step pain eases with load preparedness: calf and foot work before you stand up.

name: Pain on the outside of your elbow
explanation: Gripping and lifting may irritate the muscles attaching to the outer elbow. Adjust the grip load and rebuild wrist strength.
course: Often improves over several weeks with a manageable, consistent routine. Persistent symptoms can still improve; progress is not always linear.
helps: Start with a dose you can recover from. Use the next-morning response to guide load, then build strength gradually.
cue: Grip and wrist extension load the tender spot. We work the wrist with the elbow bent.

name: Pain on the inside of your elbow
explanation: Pulling and wrist bending can irritate the inner elbow. Gradual forearm loading and activity changes can build tolerance.
course: Often improves over several weeks with a manageable, consistent routine. Persistent symptoms can still improve; progress is not always linear.
helps: Start with a dose you can recover from. Use the next-morning response to guide load, then build strength gradually.
cue: Same logic as the outer elbow: less stretch, more steady load, and the grip gets easier.

name: Pain on the thumb side of your wrist
explanation: Thumb and wrist tendons can become sensitive with repetitive use. Reduce prolonged pinching and begin comfortable movement.
course: Often improves over several weeks with a manageable, consistent routine. Persistent symptoms can still improve; progress is not always linear.
helps: Start with a dose you can recover from. Use the next-morning response to guide load, then build strength gradually.
cue: Lifting with the thumb out to the side is what flares it. We keep the thumb in line.

name: Tingling into the hand
explanation: A sensitive nerve at the wrist can cause hand tingling, often at night. Keep the wrist comfortable and seek assessment for persistent numbness or weakness.
course: Often improves over several weeks with a manageable, consistent routine. Persistent symptoms can still improve; progress is not always linear.
helps: Start with a dose you can recover from. Use the next-morning response to guide load, then build strength gradually.
cue: Nerve symptoms need positions that unload them: we avoid end-range wrist flexion and extension.

name: A stiff, sensitive upper back
explanation: Your upper back can become sensitive to sustained positions and unfamiliar loads. Easy rotation, breathing and strength can help.
course: Often improves over several weeks with a manageable, consistent routine. Persistent symptoms can still improve; progress is not always linear.
helps: Start with a dose you can recover from. Use the next-morning response to guide load, then build strength gradually.
cue: The upper back is stiff because it is unloaded, not because it is fragile.

name: Rib-area pain with movement
explanation: Muscles and joints around the ribs can become sensitive to twisting and deep breathing. Keep movement easy; chest pain or breathlessness needs prompt assessment.
course: Often improves over several weeks with a manageable, consistent routine. Persistent symptoms can still improve; progress is not always linear.
helps: Start with a dose you can recover from. Use the next-morning response to guide load, then build strength gradually.
cue: Breathing is the treatment here: a shallow rib cage keeps the area guarded.

name: Tummy and back muscles that have switched off
explanation: Your symptoms sit in the trunk muscles rather than the spine itself. Breathing, gentle bracing and steady loading usually settle it.
course: Often improves within a few weeks once the trunk muscles are used consistently rather than hard.
helps: Short, frequent sessions. Stop before form breaks down, not when it hurts.
cue: The tummy muscles work with the back, not against it. We start with breathing and bracing.

name: Pain around the shoulder blade
explanation: The blade has to glide for the arm to work. When it sticks, the shoulder and neck both take the load.
course: Responds well to a few weeks of controlled movement and loading.
helps: Move the blade, then load it. Posture cues alone rarely fix this.
cue: The blade has to move freely before the arm can be strong.

name: A shoulder that feels insecure
explanation: After a sprain or a dislocation the shoulder often feels loose or guards itself. We build steadiness in the arc where you feel safe.
course: Confidence in the shoulder usually returns gradually over 6–12 weeks of steady loading.
helps: Keep the arm in front of you at first. Avoid end-range external rotation with load.
cue: A shoulder that has felt loose is trained in the safe arc, with the arm in front of the body.

name: Pain on the outside of the knee or thigh
explanation: The band down the outside of the thigh gets loaded heavily when the hip muscles do less work. It settles with hip strength and a temporary reduction in volume.
course: Usually improves over 4–8 weeks when running or walking load is cut back and rebuilt.
helps: Reduce distance first, then strengthen the hip. Stretching the band itself changes little.
cue: The outer knee usually settles when the hip muscles take more of the work.

name: Back of the thigh, sore when you push off
explanation: The hamstring is usually irritated at its muscle belly or near the sit bone. It heals best under gradual load, not rest and stretching.
course: Expect 3–6 weeks for a simple strain; heavier ones take longer.
helps: Isometrics early, slow lengthening under load later. Avoid aggressive stretching for a week.
cue: Early stretching is what turns a short strain into a long one. We load it gently instead.

name: Thigh muscle ache after activity
explanation: Front, side or back of the thigh, usually reproduced by the same contraction that hurt it. Capacity, not damage, is the limiting factor.
course: Typically settles in 2–4 weeks with steady loading.
helps: Keep the muscle working through the range that does not sharp-pain.
cue: Ache on the squeeze is fine; sharp pain at the same spot means we shorten the lever.

name: Pinching at the front of the hip
explanation: A pinch at a fixed angle is usually the soft tissues being compressed, not damage. Working around the pinch keeps things moving.
course: Settles over a few weeks when the provocative angle is respected.
helps: Stop short of the pinch, then extend the range weekly.
cue: Front-of-hip pinching means we stop short of the pinch and work around it.

name: An ankle that keeps going over
explanation: After repeated sprains the ankle reacts more slowly than it needs to. Balance and peroneal work is the treatment.
course: Neuromuscular gains build over 6–8 weeks of short daily practice.
helps: Practice balance on soft surfaces, progress to turning and landing.
cue: Giving way is a control problem, so we train control on unstable ground progressively.

name: Shin pain that builds with impact
explanation: Pain along the inner shin that worsens with running is a load-tolerance problem. Bone stress needs load removed early, not pushed through.
course: A few weeks of reduced impact plus calf and hip capacity usually settles it.
helps: Reduce impact now, keep non-impact fitness, rebuild distance slowly.
cue: Pain along the shin that is worse with impact needs load reduced now, then rebuilt carefully.

name: Ball of the foot or toes
explanation: Forefoot pain is usually about load under the metatarsal heads and how stiff the big toe is. Foot and calf work helps; so does the shoe.
course: Improves over several weeks once the load pattern changes.
helps: Calf strength, toe movement, and shoes that bend where your foot bends.
cue: Toe and ball-of-foot pain responds to calf work and to shoes that bend where you bend.

name: Back of the elbow when you straighten under load
explanation: The triceps insertion is loaded most at the end of straightening, so early work happens in mid-range.
course: Tendon-type symptoms: expect several weeks of steady load.
helps: Bent-elbow loading first, gradual straightening under load later.
cue: Straightening under load is the sore movement, so we build in the middle of the range first.

name: Front of shoulder and elbow that ache together
explanation: The biceps tendon crosses both joints, so overhead load aggravates the shoulder and the elbow at once.
course: Usually settles in 4–8 weeks with graded loading.
helps: Reduce overhead volume, strengthen elbow flexion in mid-range.
cue: Front-of-shoulder and elbow ache usually shares one cause: overhead loading too early.

name: Wrist pain when you push through it
explanation: Weight-bearing with the wrist bent back concentrates load on the small bones on the back of the wrist.
course: A few weeks of graded wrist loading, often with a brace for the aggravating activity.
helps: Keep the wrist straight when loading, build tolerance gradually.
cue: Weight-bearing through a bent-back wrist is the aggravator. We build the same load upright first.

name: Stiff fingers and hand
explanation: The hand loses movement quickly and regains it with repetition. Tendon gliding and gentle grip work keep things moving.
course: Consistency matters more than intensity; several short sessions a day.
helps: Move it often, avoid forcing a fist, warm the hand first.
cue: Tendon gliding keeps the fingers moving; forcing a fist is what makes the morning worse.

name: Chest wall pain with movement or breathing
explanation: The joints where the ribs meet the breastbone are commonly tender and reproducible to touch. It is uncomfortable rather than dangerous — but chest symptoms still get checked.
course: Often settles in a few weeks with movement and breathing work.
helps: Deep breaths at your own pace, gentle opening, and an assessment if it is not clearly muscular.
cue: Chest wall pain is common and benign, but chest symptoms always get checked first.

name: Jaw joint that clicks, aches or locks
explanation: The jaw joint and the muscles of chewing are closely linked to neck posture and clenching. Position and habit changes do most of the work.
course: Varies; many settle with a few weeks of rest positions and stress management.
helps: Teeth apart, tongue on the roof of the mouth, soft diet for a week, and an assessment if it locks.
cue: Jaw patterns are managed with rest positions, not exercise machines: keep teeth apart.

name: Head and face discomfort
explanation: Pain in the face, scalp or ear is usually not a muscle-joint problem that an exercise programme can fix. Neck-related headache is the exception, and we do treat that.
course: Depends entirely on the cause.
helps: If it came on suddenly and severely, or with visual or neurological change, seek care now.
cue: These areas are usually not a muscle-joint problem, so we point you somewhere useful instead.

name: Front of the neck or throat
explanation: Tenderness or a lump at the front of the neck needs a clinician rather than exercises. Neck movement from behind is often the actual source and we can treat that.
course: Not an exercise-responsive pattern in most cases.
helps: Get it assessed, especially with swallowing change, swelling or a persistent lump.
cue: Front-of-neck symptoms need a person looking, not a programme.

name: Tummy-area discomfort
explanation: Pain inside the abdomen is usually from organs rather than the wall. Muscle and nerve pain in the tummy wall does exist, and we can treat that after a clinician agrees.
course: Depends on the cause.
helps: New, severe, one-sided with a bulge, or with fever or bowel change: get seen.
cue: Tummy symptoms are usually not musculoskeletal. Here is what to watch and when to seek help.

name: Tip of the elbow, swollen or warm
explanation: The bursa at the tip of the elbow swells after leaning or a knock. Sometimes it becomes infected, which is not an exercise problem.
course: Simple bursitis settles over weeks once the pressure is removed.
helps: Stop leaning on it. If it is hot, red or you feel unwell, get seen today.
cue: Back-of-elbow swelling or warmth needs assessment; leaning on it is the thing to stop.
